chunks: "I'd split it into two phases. In the first phase the low-side switch is on.
That connects the far end of the inductor to ground, so the whole input voltage sits across the inductor and its current ramps up at V in over L .
The diode is reverse-biased because the output is higher than the switch node, so the output capacitor alone is feeding the load and its voltage droops a little.
In the second phase the switch turns off. The inductor current can't stop, so the switch node rises until the diode conducts.
Now the inductor current flows through the diode into the output capacitor and the load. The inductor voltage is V in-V out , which is negative, so the current ramps down.
The capacitor gets recharged, and its ripple is set by that pulsed current.
At steady state the current ramps up and down by the same amount each cycle, which gives V out equals V in over (1-D) .
The controller senses the output through a feedback divider and nudges the duty cycle up or down to hold it.
At light load the inductor current can reach zero before the cycle ends, which is discontinuous mode, and the switch node starts to ring."
